channel.title: Sweet Escape Blog
channel.description: Frozen-dessert guides and shop updates from Sweet Escape in Memphis, Tennessee.

item.title: Why Does Ice Melt Faster on Metal That Feels Cold?
item.description: Room-temperature metal can feel cooler than plastic yet melt ice faster. A simple test shows why, and what changes when the ice is an ice cream scoop.

item.title: Why Do Peaches Have Fuzz but Nectarines Don’t?
item.description: A nectarine is a smooth-skinned peach. Find out what peach fuzz is, why scientists shaved peaches, and what the skin tells you about a frozen dessert.

item.title: Why Did Ice Cream Once Look Like George Washington?
item.description: A Memphis museum has a mold for George Washington ice cream. See how dessert makers shaped frozen portraits, dolphins, and even a Statue of Liberty.

item.title: Why Can Cool Weather Make Blood Oranges Redder?
item.description: Why do blood oranges turn red? See how cool conditions affect their pigments, how Cara Cara differs, and where sorbetto fits into the story.

item.title: Why a Cinnamon Roll Swirl Isn’t an Ice Cream Ripple
item.description: A cinnamon roll is a sliced spiral, but an ice cream ripple can start as a moving stream. Explore both shapes and Sweet Escape’s Cinnamon Roll Sundae.

item.title: Does Pumpkin Pie Need a Carving Pumpkin?
item.description: Pie pumpkins do not always look like jack-o’-lanterns. Explore squash species, canned pumpkin labels, and Sweet Escape’s Pumpkin Pie ice cream.

item.title: Why Can Ice Cream Feel Sandy?
item.description: Ice cream can feel sandy when milk sugar forms crystals. Learn how lactose differs from ice, what researchers measured, and why particle size matters.

item.title: The Ice Cream Stick Had a Job Before You Held It
item.description: Early ice cream bars and ice pops used their sticks for more than eating. Original patents reveal how the handles helped with coating and mold release.

item.title: Green and Black Tea Can Come From the Same Plant
item.description: Green and black tea can start with the same plant. Discover how leaf processing, shade and milling lead to different teas—and a Sweet Escape matcha connection.

item.title: What Was a Penny Lick? Ice Cream’s Tiny Glass
item.description: Ice cream once came in tiny reusable glasses called penny licks. Explore their shallow bowls, museum clues, street sellers, and a surprising serving history.

item.title: Scientists Used a Particle Accelerator to Study Ice Cream
item.description: Scientists brought ice cream to a particle accelerator to see its hidden structure. Explore 3D X-ray scans, changing air bubbles, and a tiny frozen experiment.

item.title: Honeybees Dance Directions to Food
item.description: Honeybees can dance a food source’s direction and distance. Explore sun-based signals, learning, radar research, and a verified Sweet Escape gelato connection.

item.title: Why Does Mochi Ice Cream Have a Soft Wrapper?
item.description: Explore mochi ice cream’s rice-cake wrapper: sticky-rice starch, soft-texture research, a warm-to-cold forming puzzle, and two development histories.

item.title: Why Doesn’t Churning Ice Cream Just Make Butter?
item.description: Ice cream and butter share a surprising fat-structure story. Learn how controlled clustering helps a scoop and why butter-making reaches a different endpoint.

item.title: Blueberries Have a Blue Trick Hidden in Their Wax
item.description: Why are blueberries blue when their juice is not? Explore the wax-coating science, pigment chemistry, and a careful Blueberry Burst ice cream connection.

item.title: The Malt in a Milkshake Starts With Sprouted Grain
item.description: Malt begins with a grain starting to grow. Explore malting, malted milk powder, an 1883 patent, and the difference between drink mixes and baking malts.

item.title: A Freezer Warms the Room While It Chills Ice Cream
item.description: Why does a freezer release heat while keeping ice cream cold? Follow the cooling cycle, a simple energy example, and the open-door room-cooling puzzle.

item.title: Maraschino Cherries Aren’t a Cherry-Tree Variety
item.description: The cherry on top has a surprising backstory: brine, texture research, radish color experiments, and even a dated attempt to turn leftovers into fuel.

item.title: The Ice Cream Sundae Has a Birthplace Rivalry
item.description: Two cities tell different ice cream sundae origin stories. Explore chocolate syrup, Cherry Sunday ads, curious spelling, and a Tennessee stamp connection.

item.title: Spaghetti Ice Cream Is Real—But It Isn’t Pasta
item.description: Discover the Mannheim story behind spaghetti ice cream, how its sweet ingredients imitate pasta, and what food-presentation studies can—and cannot—tell us.
